title: Bandwidth fair-share prefetch prototype
content:
Summary:

This note captures the design and early lab results for a prototype that enforces memory-channel bandwidth fair-share across concurrent tenants while adapting prefetch window sizes per-tenant. The goal is to reduce cross-tenant tail latency spikes caused by KV-prefetch storms and uneven channel saturation, without sacrificing reuse-driven cache hit-rate benefits for latency-sensitive tenants.

Motivation / observed problem:
- On mixed workloads (many short-chat requests + a few long-context batch completions) we see periodic tail latency spikes for short requests (~95-99th pct) correlated with one or two tenants generating sustained KV reads that saturate a subset of memory channels.
- Traditional LRU-style eviction combined with naive prefetch widens the problem: aggressive prefetch from noisy tenants causes bandwidth contention and increases page fault latency for other tenants that rely on low-latency KV hits.
- Existing bank/channel pinning experiments reduced worst-case interference, but either underutilize bandwidth (over-isolation) or are static and fail to adapt to workload transitions.

Hypothesis:
1) A lightweight bandwidth-crediting layer at the memory-channel level, combined with per-tenant adaptive prefetch windows (scale with observed local reuse score), will reduce cross-tenant tail latency without materially reducing overall cache hit-rate.
2) Fair-share allocation based on recent per-tenant observed reuse density (tokens/sec of hot-keys) will prioritize tenants that get most value from cache bandwidth while throttling streaming/scan-y tenants.

Testbed and instrumentation:
- Hardware: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs with 4 memory-channel NICs exposed in our NVMe-backed prototyping rig (same node topology as serving-runtime test rig).
- Software branch: runtime/feature/bw-fair-prefetch-proto (PR linked in artifacts).
- Workloads:
  * short-chat (SC): 128ms median service, seqlen ~80, high qps (simulates chat UI).
  * long-stream (LS): long generation requests with high KV-read density, seqlen ~2048, lower qps but sustained KV reads.
  * background-embedding (BE): embedding-style workload causing sequential KV scanning from large context (low reuse).
- Mixed scenarios: 70% SC + 20% LS + 10% BE (primary), also stress runs with 50/30/20 and tenant-only baselines.
- Metrics collected: per-tenant 50/95/99/99.9 latency, KV hit-rate, read iops, bytes/sec per memory channel, page fault count, prefetch requests/sec, reuse_rate (recent unique hits / total reads), tail_latency_impact (delta vs baseline).

Algorithm (prototype summary):
- Bandwidth Fair-Share Throttler (BFS-T):
  1) Every 250ms sample window, measure bytes/sec per tenant aggregated across channels and compute each tenant's recent locality_score = exponential_moving_avg(reuse_rate, alpha=0.25).
  2) Compute fair bandwidth allocation: B_total = measured BW headroom (targeted to keep <85% channel utilization). For each tenant i, allocate B_i = clamp( base_share + locality_score_i * locality_weight, min_share, max_share ). base_share=5% of B_total, locality_weight tuned to bias locality-sensitive tenants.
  3) Enforce allocation by throttling prefetch issuance and read concurrency tokens per-tenant. Prefetch window size is scaled proportionally to allocated B_i; streaming tenants receive smaller windows and tighter concurrency limits.
  4) Emergency fallback: if overall channel utilization drops below 60% but miss-rate spikes, gradually relax prefetch constraints.

Prototype-specific details / heuristics tested:
- Two throttling knobs tested: prefetch-window-size (number of KV pages prefetched ahead) and read-concurrency (max in-flight read RPCs).
- Locality_score computed over last 30s with decay; provides stability across short bursts.
- min_share=2% B_total per tenant, max_share=60% to avoid total domination.
- Rapid tenant transitions: added a short-term burst bucket (burst credits) to allow tenants coming from idle to warm quickly for one sample window, then revert to allocation.

Experiment runs and results (primary mixed scenario 70/20/10):
- Baselines: static-prefetch (current mainline), channel-pinning (experiment), BFS-T prototype.
- Summary numbers (values are medians across 5 runs, each run 2 hours):
  * Short-chat 99th latency: static-prefetch 840ms, channel-pinning 610ms, BFS-T 320ms
  * Short-chat 99.9th latency: static-prefetch 1270ms, channel-pinning 900ms, BFS-T 480ms
  * KV hit-rate (overall): static-prefetch 78%, channel-pinning 75%, BFS-T 73%
  * System-wide bytes/sec utilization: static 92% (frequent saturation), channel-pinning 68%, BFS-T 81%
  * Background-embedding throughput (requests/min): static 1000, channel-pinning 640, BFS-T 820
  * Page faults (total): static 5400, channel-pinning 2100, BFS-T 2400

Interpretation:
- BFS-T substantially reduces tail latencies for latency-sensitive short-chat tenants (approx 60% reduction at 99.9th) compared to static prefetching, while keeping overall bandwidth utilization high (~81%).
- The hit-rate drop (78% -> 73%) is expected — BFS-T trades some hit-rate for improved latency predictability. The net user-visible latency improvement for SC tenants is large, which matches product priorities for interactive workloads.
- Channel-pinning gave good isolation but left headroom unused (68% utilization), lowering throughput for background tenants. BFS-T makes a better utilization vs fairness tradeoff by dynamically shifting credits toward high-locality tenants.
- Burst credits and the <85% utilization target were important to avoid cold-start penalty for tenants coming online.

Micro-observations and anomalies:
- Short transient regressions (~1–2 min) were observed when a single LS tenant ramped from 0 -> sustained streaming: our burst credit decay was too quick in one run causing a local spike in page faults. Increased burst-decay from 1s to 5s mitigated.
- We saw per-channel imbalance when tenants aggressively pinned prefetched pages to a preferred channel; next iteration should include channel-aware allocation to avoid creating hot channels.
- In a couple of runs, GC/pinning interactions in the runtime caused slower recovery post-faults; we need to instrument object lifetimes around prefetch queue nodes.

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: add a per-tenant bandwidth_allocated metric + prefetch_window_histogram. Also expose locality_score and prefetch_denials counters for SRE dashboards.
- Safety: start with conservative knobs (min_share 3%, locality_weight small) behind a kill-switch. Gradually increase on dedicated pilot clusters.
- Canary strategy: 1) low-traffic dedicated cluster, 2) percentage rollout by tenant tier, 3) full region. Monitor 95/99/99.9 and page-fault delta.

Next steps / action items:
- (Jordan) clean up branch and add feature flag + metrics instrumentation (PR 842 has prototype code; need unit tests) — ETA 2025-02-25.
- (Aisha) run a 24-hour long mixed-run with live customer-like traces from prod-traffic-sim — ETA 2025-03-03.
- (Miguel) prototype channel-aware allocator to avoid single-channel hot spots — ETA 2025-03-10.
- (Sana) draft rollout plan and required SLO guardrails for gradual enablement — ETA 2025-02-28.

Risks and open questions:
- How will BFS-T interact with Dedicated instances where tenants correspond to internal customers? We need policy decisions: should dedicated tenants get isolation override?
- Cost implications: slightly lower hit-rate could increase egress read cost; need to model cost per token change for real customer mixes.
- Security: per-tenant telemetry must be scrubbed of any identifiable payloads.

Appendix: lightweight pseudocode (trimmed)

function sample_and_allocate():
  samples = collect_per_tenant_bw_and_reuse(250ms)
  B_total = compute_bandwidth_headroom(target_util=0.85)
  for tenant in samples:
    locality = ema(tenant.reuse_rate, alpha=0.25)
    alloc[tenant] = clamp(min_share, base_share + locality*locality_weight, max_share) * B_total
  return alloc

function serve_request(req):
  tenant = req.tenant
  if current_alloc[tenant] < prefetch_cost_estimate(req):
    deny_prefetch(req) // force on-demand read for small requests
  else:
    issue_prefetch(req, scaled_window_for(tenant))

Closing note:
This prototype looks promising as a middle ground between static isolation and uncontrolled prefetch. The trade-off surface (hit-rate vs tail latency vs utilization) aligns with product goals: prioritize lower tail latency for interactive tenants while keeping cluster-level efficiency reasonable. The next milestone is a longer-duration trace-driven test to validate stability and to gather cost-model inputs for product decisions.
